topic.en: Three texts: how earthquake waves revealed the inside of the Earth, how the jet engine works, and the argument about releasing gene-edited mosquitoes.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: сейсмикалық толқындар Жердің ішкі құрылысын қалай көрсетті, реактивті қозғалтқыш қалай жұмыс істейді және гені өзгертілген масаларды жіберу туралы талқы.
topic.ru: Три текста: как сейсмические волны показали устройство недр Земли, как устроен реактивный двигатель, и спор о выпуске генетически изменённых комаров.

paragraphs.text: No one has ever seen the interior of the Earth. The deepest hole ever drilled, on a peninsula in the far north of Europe, reached a little over twelve kilometres before the rising heat made further progress impossible, which is less than a fifth of one per cent of the distance to the centre of the planet. Yet geologists can describe the structure of the interior in considerable detail, from the thin rocky crust through the vast mantle to a core of iron at the centre. Almost everything they know has been learned indirectly, by studying the way earthquake waves travel through the planet. Even the crust beneath the oceans, which is much thinner than that under the continents, has never been drilled through completely, and the deepest borehole was eventually abandoned and sealed.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: When an earthquake occurs, it sends out several kinds of waves. Some, known as primary waves, compress and stretch the rock in the direction in which they travel, much as sound moves through air, and they can pass through solids, liquids and gases. Others, known as secondary waves, shake the rock from side to side, and they can travel only through solids. Primary waves travel faster and arrive first at a distant recording station, and the difference in arrival times between the two kinds allows seismologists to work out how far away an earthquake occurred. A third kind, surface waves, travels along the outside of the planet and usually causes most of the damage.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The speed of these waves depends on the properties of the rock they pass through, and when they cross a boundary between different materials they bend and are partly reflected, just as light does when it passes from air into water. By comparing records from stations around the world, early seismologists found that waves were travelling along curved paths and arriving at unexpected times, patterns that could be explained only if the interior were made of layers with different properties. The principle had been suggested earlier, but reliable instruments were needed to test it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The most striking discovery came from a gap in the records. Beyond a certain distance from any large earthquake, stations on the opposite side of the planet received no secondary waves at all, and primary waves arrived later than expected. Scientists concluded in the early twentieth century that the Earth has a core whose outer part is liquid, since secondary waves cannot pass through liquid, and which bends primary waves sharply. The shadow cast by the core on the far side of the planet allowed its size to be calculated with remarkable accuracy. The boundary between the mantle and the core lies nearly three thousand kilometres below the surface.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A further surprise followed in 1936. A Danish seismologist, studying faint primary waves that appeared within the shadow zone where none were expected, proposed that they had been reflected from a solid inner core within the liquid outer core. Her interpretation was later confirmed, and the inner core is now known to be a ball of iron and nickel roughly the size of the moon, solid despite temperatures comparable to those on the surface of the sun because the enormous pressure keeps it from melting. Her work was carried out largely by hand, comparing thousands of printed records.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Knowledge of the interior has become far more detailed as the number of seismometers has grown. By combining millions of records, researchers now produce three-dimensional images of the mantle, in a technique similar to the scans used in medicine. These images reveal regions where waves travel faster or slower than average, which are interpreted as colder or hotter rock. They show slabs of ocean floor sinking deep into the mantle at the edges of continents and broad columns of hot material rising beneath some volcanic islands. The images are still blurred in places where few earthquakes occur or few instruments are installed, and the same methods are used on a small scale by companies searching for oil and gas.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Other evidence supports the picture built from earthquakes. The average density of the Earth, calculated from its gravity, is much greater than that of surface rocks, which implies that heavier material must lie at depth. Meteorites, thought to be fragments of bodies similar to those from which the planet formed, include some made largely of iron and nickel. Experiments in which tiny samples are squeezed between diamonds to pressures found deep inside the Earth help to show how minerals behave under such conditions. Laboratory results sometimes disagree with seismic observations, which has led to revisions of both.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The liquid outer core is also responsible for one of the most important features of the planet. The movement of molten iron within it generates the magnetic field that surrounds the Earth and shields its surface from much of the radiation arriving from space. The field changes slowly over time and has reversed its direction many times in the past, and seismology continues to provide clues about the processes deep inside the core that drive these changes. Seismometers have also been placed on the moon and on Mars, allowing the same methods to be used on other worlds.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: The jet engine transformed travel more thoroughly than almost any other invention of the twentieth century. Within a few decades of the first jet-powered flights in the late 1930s, jet aircraft had replaced propeller planes on most long-distance routes, cutting journey times in half and making international travel available to millions of people. The engine that made this possible has changed enormously since then, becoming far quieter, more reliable and more efficient, but its basic principle has remained the same. Its development was driven at first by military needs, and the first engines were unreliable and short-lived.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: That principle is simple: air is drawn in at the front, compressed, mixed with fuel and burned, and the hot gas is expelled at high speed from the back, pushing the engine forward in reaction. In the earliest engines, known as turbojets, all the air passed through the combustion chamber. A turbine placed behind the chamber extracted some of the energy of the hot gas to drive the compressor at the front, while the rest emerged as a fast, narrow jet that produced thrust. Some aircraft designed for very high speeds still use engines close to this original design.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Turbojets were powerful but inefficient and extremely loud, because most of their thrust came from a small amount of gas moving very fast. Engineers realised that the same thrust could be produced more economically by moving a larger mass of air more slowly. The solution was the turbofan, in which a large fan at the front drives most of the incoming air around the outside of the engine core rather than through it. This bypass air produces most of the thrust in a modern airliner engine and also surrounds the hot core exhaust, reducing noise considerably. The idea had been proposed early in the history of the jet engine but became practical only as materials improved, and noise near airports has fallen dramatically as a result.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The proportion of air that bypasses the core, known as the bypass ratio, has risen steadily. Early turbofans sent roughly equal amounts of air around and through the core; in the largest modern engines, around ten times as much air passes around the core as through it. The fans have become correspondingly larger, and on some engines their diameter is now greater than the width of the aircraft cabin behind them. Larger fans improve fuel efficiency, but they are heavier and harder to fit beneath the wings, which limits how far the ratio can be increased on existing aircraft designs. Some engines use a gearbox between the fan and the turbine, allowing each to turn at its most efficient speed.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The heart of the engine faces extreme conditions. Gas leaving the combustion chamber is hotter than the melting point of the metal alloys from which the first turbine blades are made. The blades survive only because they are cooled by air passed through tiny internal channels and out through holes in their surface, forming a thin protective film, and because they are coated with ceramic layers that insulate them from the heat. Many are grown as a single crystal of metal, without the boundaries between crystals that would otherwise weaken them at high temperatures. Manufacturing such blades is one of the most demanding processes in engineering, and a single blade can be worth as much as a family car.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: These improvements have produced dramatic gains. A modern airliner uses roughly half as much fuel per passenger-kilometre as the first generation of jet airliners, and engines now run for tens of thousands of hours between major overhauls. Sensors throughout the engine transmit data during flight, allowing maintenance teams to detect wear and plan repairs before faults develop. Twin-engine aircraft are now permitted to fly routes far from the nearest airport that were once reserved for aircraft with three or four engines, a reflection of how reliable engines have become. Much of this reliability comes from careful analysis of every fault that occurs anywhere in the world.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Aviation nonetheless remains one of the most difficult sources of greenhouse gases to reduce. Kerosene stores a great deal of energy for its weight, and no battery comes close to matching it, which rules out electric power for long flights in the foreseeable future. Manufacturers are working on engines with even larger, open fans without an outer casing, which could reduce fuel use further, and on engines that can burn fuels made from waste or plants, or hydrogen, although each option faces significant obstacles of cost, supply or storage. Improvements in air traffic management, allowing aircraft to fly more direct routes, could also reduce fuel use.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The history of the jet engine illustrates how a technology can improve enormously through steady refinement rather than dramatic breakthroughs. Most of the gains of the past sixty years came from better materials, more precise manufacturing and a gradual increase in the size of the fan. Whether similar refinement can produce the much larger reductions in emissions that are now required is one of the central questions facing the aviation industry. Engineers who work on the next generation of engines are therefore looking beyond the traditional design.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Mosquitoes are responsible for more human illness than any other animal, not through their bites themselves but through the diseases they carry. Malaria alone affects hundreds of millions of people a year, most of them in Africa. Bed nets, insecticides and medicines have reduced its toll substantially, but progress has slowed as mosquitoes have become resistant to insecticides and the parasite to drugs. Against this background, a genetic technology known as a gene drive has been proposed as a way of reducing or altering mosquito populations across entire regions, and it has provoked one of the most serious debates in modern biology. Other mosquito-borne diseases, including dengue and several viral infections, have spread to new regions as the climate warms, and supporters and critics agree that the stakes are unusually high.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ordinarily, a gene carried by one parent has a fifty per cent chance of being passed to each offspring, so a new genetic trait introduced into a small number of insects would spread only if it gave them an advantage. A gene drive overrides this rule. It includes the machinery for copying itself onto the matching chromosome from the other parent, so that almost all offspring inherit it. Released into a population, a drive can spread through it within a few years even if it harms the insects that carry it, for example by making females infertile. The idea was proposed decades ago, but became practical only with the arrival of precise gene-editing tools.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Amina Diallo, an entomologist who has worked on such projects, argues that the technology offers something no existing method can: a self-sustaining intervention that reaches mosquitoes in places where spraying and nets cannot. She points out that only a few of the several hundred mosquito species in Africa carry malaria to humans, and a drive could be designed to target those species alone. Cage experiments have shown that a drive can eliminate a population of a malaria-carrying species within a year. She adds that a drive could reach remote areas that health workers visit only rarely, and because it spreads by itself, it could also be cheaper than repeated spraying.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The ecological consequences are the main concern. Henrik Larsen, an ecologist, notes that little is known about which animals depend on the targeted species for food, or which other insects might fill the space they leave. Because a drive is designed to spread and persist, a release could not easily be reversed if unexpected effects appeared. He does not argue that the risks are necessarily large, but insists that they have not yet been studied sufficiently, and that field trials should proceed in careful stages, beginning with drives that are designed to stop spreading after a limited number of generations. Some researchers have proposed drives that alter mosquitoes so that they cannot carry the parasite, rather than reducing their numbers.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Resistance may also limit the technology. In several laboratory studies, mosquitoes evolved changes in the DNA targeted by the drive that prevented it from copying itself, allowing resistant insects to survive and multiply. Researchers have responded by designing drives that target sequences which cannot change without harming the mosquito, and by combining several targets in a single drive. Diallo is confident that these improvements will work, but acknowledges that behaviour in the wild may differ from that in cages. Larger cage trials, designed to imitate natural conditions more closely, are under way.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Decisions about release raise difficult questions of consent. Mosquitoes do not respect borders, so a drive released in one country would almost certainly spread to its neighbours. Maya Patel, a bioethicist, argues that communities living in the areas concerned must have a genuine voice in whether and how releases occur, not merely be informed after decisions are made elsewhere. She notes that several projects have spent years consulting local communities, and regards this as a model, but warns that no international body currently has clear authority to approve or refuse a release. Legal frameworks for such decisions differ widely between countries.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Supporters in the countries most affected sometimes express frustration with these objections. Joseph Kariuki, a public health official, points out that every year of delay has a human cost, and that the risks of doing nothing are certain while the risks of the technology are speculative. He accepts the need for careful testing but argues that the decision should be taken primarily by the countries that bear the burden of the disease, rather than by researchers and regulators in places where malaria no longer exists. He also notes that people in affected regions have often been more supportive of the research than outsiders expected.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The debate over gene drives brings together scientific uncertainty, ecological caution and questions of justice. A technology that could prevent a great deal of illness also has the capacity to alter ecosystems permanently and across borders. Proceeding in stages, with independent assessment and the involvement of the communities affected, appears to be the only way of testing whether the promise can be realised without unacceptable harm, and it is the path that most current projects say they are following. Few technologies have forced scientists to think so carefully about consent before the first release.
paragraphs.label: H
